title: Jesus as God in the New Testament
short: Jesus as God in the NT

keyTerms.d: Richard Bauckham’s phrase for what the New Testament does repeatedly and across independent authors: including Jesus within the unique identity of the one God of Israel — placing him on the Creator’s side of the line that Jewish monotheism drew between God and everything else. The framework is influential but not uncontested: James D. G. Dunn and, from a different angle, James F. McGrath question how sharply that boundary can be drawn.

Old Testament passages about the LORD himself, applied without apology to Jesus: Isaiah 45’s every-knee-shall-bow in the Philippians hymn, Joel’s “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord” in Romans 10 (on the most natural reading of Paul’s argument), Psalm 102’s unchanging Creator in Hebrews 1, Isaiah’s “the first and the last” in Revelation.

A text that does not merely place Jesus on the Creator’s side of the line but calls him theos, “God,” directly. Two depend on neither the Granville Sharp rule nor a disputed comma — Thomas’s confession, which no grammatical alternative touches, and Hebrews’ “O God,” which rests on the reading its own chapter’s argument favours — and they are the ones worth resting weight on.

The grammatical rule on which Titus 2:13 (“our great God and Savior Jesus Christ”) and 2 Peter 1:1 turn; Daniel Wallace argues it holds without exception in native Koine when its conditions are properly met. Translators have not always agreed, and the grammar is genuinely contested — the weakest leg of the argument, not its foundation.

Larry Hurtado’s term for the pattern of devotional practice that emerged “amazingly early,” among Jewish believers who would have regarded worshiping any creature as blasphemy: they sang to Christ, baptized into his name, called on his name, broke bread in his presence, and prayed to him — while insisting, with the Shema, that God is one.

An Aramaic prayer Paul preserves untranslated in his Greek-speaking churches: “Our Lord, come!” That it survives in Aramaic is the point — it carries us back behind Paul’s Greek to the Aramaic-speaking Judean church. It is not the homage due a vice-regent; it is an invocation, that is, prayer.

The reading of Jehovah’s Witnesses and biblical Unitarians, drawn from the Hebrew Bible: an emissary can bear the sender’s name and authority — the angel of the LORD speaks as God, Moses is made “like God to Pharaoh” — without being the LORD. The motif is genuinely present in the Hebrew Bible, but it cannot bear the weight put on it: it breaks at one point — cultic worship.

Bart Ehrman’s case that the earliest followers held an “exaltation” Christology and that the elevation to the co-equal God confessed at Nicaea was the later step. He also finds a pre-existent Christ in material older than Paul, so what he says developed was the divine figure’s rank, not the date of pre-existence itself.

derive.q: Some twenty-seven documents, perhaps nine or ten authors, roughly half a century, two languages, scattered communities that never coordinated their theology — and they converge on the same inclusion. So the convergence is…?
derive.ans: hard to explain as coincidence or gradual drift
derive.why: Pick up any individual verse and a determined reader can propose another reading. But the New Testament is not a single verse. The convergence of independent authors on the same astonishing inclusion is hard to explain as coincidence or gradual drift.

derive.q: A text in which the LORD swears that to him alone every knee shall bow is applied to Jesus by a monotheist Jew. So Jesus is placed…?
derive.ans: on the Creator’s side of the line
derive.why: That last phrase of the Philippians hymn is lifted from Isaiah 45, where the LORD swears that to him alone every knee shall bow — and Paul applies it to Jesus. In the same way Hebrews reads a psalm about Yahweh’s eternity and creative work, without apology, as words to Christ.

derive.q: Grant every grammatical concession on the three contested texts. What is left?
derive.ans: a floor — two direct predications still stand
derive.why: John’s confession, which no grammatical alternative touches, and Hebrews’ “O God,” which rests on the reading its own chapter’s argument favours. The “called God” case does not live or die on a disputed comma; it has a floor — John 20:28 at the least — and the floor is firm.

derive.q: An angel twice refuses worship and redirects it to God; Jesus receives it without a word of protest; the first Aramaic-speaking church prays to him. So he has…?
derive.why: What Jewish monotheism guarded jealously for God was not the posture of homage but the substance of worship — sacrifice, invocation, prayer. A figure you worship and pray to, while confessing in the same breath that God is one, has already outrun the category of “supreme agent.”

derive.q: The pattern of worship is in place within a decade or two of the crucifixion, not a century after. So what developed?
derive.why: The earliest Christians did not slowly climb a ladder from a low Christology to a high one; on Bauckham’s reading they expressed the highest possible claim from the start, using the very resources of Jewish monotheism. John is not the invention of a new doctrine but the most explicit articulation of an old one.

derive.q: Grant all of it. Does this, by itself, establish the developed creed?
derive.ans: no — it is one strand of a cumulative case
derive.why: It does not, by itself, establish the developed creed. It does not settle the disputed grammar of Romans 9:5 or prove the Trinity from a proof-text. It interlocks with the historical case for the resurrection, the witness of the earliest post-apostolic church, and the philosophical coherence of trinitarian monotheism. What it offers is the foundation those other lines build on.

honestState.p1: The “called God” case has a floor — John 20:28 at the least — and the floor is firm; Hebrews 1:8’s “O God” rests on the majority, vocative reading. Titus 2:13, 2 Peter 1:1 and Romans 9:5 turn on Greek grammar and punctuation, and the grammar is genuinely contested: this is the weakest leg of the argument, not its foundation. The weight falls on worship and divine identity — the pattern of devotion Hurtado documents is in place within a decade or two of the crucifixion, and the early date of the pre-Pauline Marana tha is not seriously contested.
honestState.fairness: Bauckham’s “divine identity” framework is influential but not uncontested: James D. G. Dunn and, from a different angle, James F. McGrath have questioned how sharply the boundary of divine identity can be drawn, and Hurtado — broadly an ally — preferred to frame the data as devotional practice rather than in Bauckham’s identity categories. The pre-Pauline dating of the Philippians hymn is itself debated (Gordon Fee argues Paul composed it), the Colossians hymn’s status and the letter’s authorship more so; and Gathercole’s case for Synoptic preexistence is a serious minority-to-moderate position, not a scholarly consensus. The most formidable academic challenge is Bart Ehrman’s developmental thesis — and Ehrman himself finds a pre-existent Christ in material older than Paul.
honestState.verdict: This establishes one strand of a cumulative argument: that the New Testament, read across its full breadth, presents Jesus as sharing the identity of the one God of Israel and as the rightful recipient of God’s worship — and that this presentation is early, widespread, and woven into the church’s earliest practice, not bolted on at the end. The New Testament does not hand us the later vocabulary of “one essence in three persons” or “two natures in one person”; the raw data the creeds later organized is already here, and the developed doctrine is the faithful articulation of it rather than a later imposition upon it. When Thomas said “My Lord and my God,” he was not inventing a category; he was naming what the whole New Testament had been saying all along.

order: The New Testament gives Jesus the names of God.
It gives him the works and worship of God.
Therefore the New Testament presents Jesus as fully God — distinct from the Father, not a second god.

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and its precision check.
cards.a: The New Testament gives Jesus the names of God: YHWH texts applied to him, the first and the last, called God outright. Precision: not the later vocabulary of “one essence” or “two natures” — the raw data the creeds later organized, distributed across the whole canon.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and its precision check.
cards.a: It gives him the works and worship of God. Precision: a gesture of homage was not itself the line — Israelites could bow before a king as well as the LORD. What Jewish monotheism guarded for God was the substance of worship: sacrifice, invocation, prayer.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That the New Testament presents Jesus as sharing the identity of the one God and as the rightful recipient of his worship — early and widespread. It does not, by itself, establish the developed creed, settle disputed grammar, or prove the Trinity from a proof-text; it is one strand of a cumulative case.

cards.q: Why does the “every knee shall bow” line in the Philippians hymn carry so much weight?
cards.a: It is lifted from a passage where the LORD swears that to him alone every knee shall bow — and Paul applies it to Jesus. A text reserved for the one God is given, by a monotheist Jew, to Jesus.

cards.q: What does Hebrews 1 do with a psalm addressed to the LORD?
cards.a: It reads a psalm about the unchanging Creator — “You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth… but you are the same” — as words to the Son. A text about Yahweh’s eternity and creative work is, without apology, read as words to Christ.

cards.q: Why does Thomas’s “My Lord and my God” form a floor no grammar dispute touches?
cards.a: The narrator frames the words as spoken to Jesus (“said to him”); the phrase functions as a vocative of direct address; and Jesus accepts the confession and blesses those who will believe without seeing, while John lets it stand as the climax of the book.

cards.q: Reply to: the “God” texts all depend on disputed grammar.
cards.a: Candor costs the case nothing. Grant every concession on the contested three and two direct predications still stand — John’s confession, which no grammatical alternative touches, and Hebrews’ “O God,” which rests on the reading its own chapter’s argument favours. The disputed grammar is the weakest leg, not the foundation; the weight falls on worship and divine identity.

cards.q: Where did Jewish monotheism draw the line — and how is Jesus treated at it?
cards.a: Not at the posture of homage but at the substance of worship. The intermediary figures characteristically refuse worship and redirect it to God; in the very books that record it an angel twice refuses John’s worship, while Jesus receives it without a word of protest.

cards.q: Why does an Aramaic two-word prayer in a Greek letter matter?
cards.a: That the invocation survives untranslated carries us back behind Paul’s Greek to the Aramaic-speaking Judean church, calling on the risen Jesus as the Lord who will come. It is prayer, not the homage due a vice-regent — the highest devotion is bedrock, not a late Hellenistic overlay.

cards.q: What one concession is owed to the developmental thesis — and where does it stop?
cards.a: The developed creedal vocabulary came later. That is all the developmental thesis’s evidence actually shows. It stops short of the leap that the deity of Christ was a late arrival: the deity is precisely what the developing vocabulary was straining to state. The development is in the clarity, not in the substance.

cards.q: Reply to: the baptism voice and “declared Son by his resurrection” show he was adopted.
cards.a: That is a reconstruction of a layer behind the texts, genuinely debated; the texts as we have them do not require it. The one “declared with power to be the Son of God by his resurrection” is already “His Son, who was a descendant of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3–4). The contrast is between the Son in the weakness of the flesh and the Son in power, not between a mere man and an adopted Son. A confirmation needs something to confirm.

cards.q: Does this case deny that Jesus was truly human?
cards.a: No. His genuine humanity — he hungers, prays, and dies — is fully affirmed alongside his deity; the historic doctrine is that he is both. The incarnation predicts exactly this two-register data: truly human, so he hungers and prays; truly God, so he creates and forgives.

obj.q: Jesus is never actually called God in the New Testament. The deity of Christ is a later church invention.
obj.model: He is — John 20:28 at the least calls him God directly. Thomas “said to him” — the narrator’s own words — “My Lord and my God,” and Jesus accepts it. More broadly, the claim is not that the New Testament states the Nicene Creed word for word; that vocabulary is later. It is that independent authors, writing across half a century in two languages, repeatedly include Jesus within the unique identity of the one God of Israel: Isaiah’s every-knee text given to him, a psalm about the unchanging Creator read as words to him, the LORD’s own “first and the last” on his lips — and the worship reserved for God alone offered to him, in prayer, by the first Aramaic-speaking church. The words for it were refined over centuries; the reality is bedrock, and it is there in the earliest layer we can reach.

obj.q: Jesus is God’s supreme agent, not God. In the Hebrew Bible an emissary bears the sender’s name and authority — the angel of the LORD speaks as God, Moses is made “like God to Pharaoh” — without being the LORD. And Jesus himself calls the Father “the only true God.”
obj.model: It is true that in the Hebrew Bible an emissary can bear the sender’s name and authority. But there is one thing no agent — not the angel of the LORD, not Moses, not the most exalted king, not even the great angels who were given God’s own name, such as Yahoel — ever receives: the cultic devotion reserved for God alone. Grant that God’s name and functions could be entrusted to a supreme agent, and the worship itself still could not be. A gesture of homage was not the line — Israelites could bow before a king as well as the LORD; what was guarded was sacrifice, invocation, prayer. An angel twice refuses the worship John offers; Jesus receives it without protest. And Marana tha is not the homage due a vice-regent — it is an invocation, calling on the risen Lord to come; that is, prayer, offered by the first Aramaic-speaking church. John 17:3 excludes the idols, not the Son; two verses later (John 17:5) the same Jesus asks for the glory he had “before the world existed” — glory that Isaiah says YHWH shares with no other. Grant the framework the titles for the sake of argument; it still breaks at the altar. So the agency reading does not hold.

obj.q: Belief in Jesus’ deity evolved. His earliest followers held an exaltation Christology; even where they saw a pre-existent figure, he was a subordinate divine being — God’s chief angel — and his elevation to the co-equal God came later.
obj.model: The developmental thesis fails. The disagreement is not really about dates — Ehrman himself finds a pre-existent Christ in material older than Paul’s letters — but about what kind of being the earliest Christians took him to be. And the evidence answers that question with the one thing the developmental thesis cannot easily accommodate: the earliest worship. Marana tha is Aramaic, pre-Pauline, rooted in the Jerusalem church of the 30s; the Philippians hymn, widely regarded as pre-Pauline, already applies an exclusive-worship text of YHWH to Jesus (its dating is debated, but the worship-of-Jesus datum stands either way); and the pattern of worship Hurtado documents is in place within a decade or two of the crucifixion, not a century after. One concession is owed: the developed creedal vocabulary came later. That much is true, and it is all Ehrman’s evidence actually shows. What it gets wrong is its leap to the conclusion that the deity of Christ was a late arrival — the deity is precisely what the developing vocabulary was straining to state. The development is in the clarity, not in the substance.

obj.q: Thomas wasn’t calling Jesus God. “My Lord and my God” was an astonished cry to heaven — an “oh my God.”
obj.model: The reply is cumulative and rests on no single word. The narrator frames the words as spoken to Jesus (“said to him”); the phrase is an articular nominative that functions as a vocative of direct address, the ordinary Greek way of calling someone “Lord” and “God”; and Jesus, far from correcting the confession, accepts it and blesses those who will believe without seeing, while John lets it stand as the climax of the book, immediately before he states why he wrote. It is no accident that the same Gospel opens with “the Word was God” and closes here: the deity of Christ is the frame around the whole work, not a stray remark inside it.

unseen.q: On the cross Jesus cries, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Someone who cries out to God, abandoned by God, can’t himself be God.
unseen.model: The Gospels place on the lips of the dying Jesus the opening cry of Psalm 22, and the case does not hide it: the one who shares the divine identity enters, on the cross, the depths of human god-forsakenness. It is the incarnate Son, in his full humanity, who suffers, dies, and cries out — so that God himself, in the person of the Son, has entered our suffering and death for us. That is not to say the divine nature suffered or changed, nor that the Father was crucified or forsaken (the ancient error of patripassianism); the Father is not the Son, and the impassible God does not perish — the cross reveals who God is, it does not make God mortal. Nor was the Son torn from the Father or the Trinity divided: the Father never ceased to love the Son, and the union of the persons was never broken. The forsakenness is real, borne in the Son’s human experience, not a severing within the one God. And the cross does not stand outside the divine identity: Isaiah’s despised and crushed Servant shall be “high and lifted up,” the very words of the LORD’s throne-vision, and John says Isaiah “saw his glory and spoke of him.” On the divine-identity reading the cry is not a lapse into something less than God but the fullest disclosure of who God is: the God who gives himself, to the uttermost, for his people.
